The '''1732 [[FLLA]] World Cup''' was the 16th edition of the [[FLLA World Cup]], the quadrennial international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the member associations of the [[FLLA]]. It was held in [[Dahe]] across [[Massir]] from 22 May to 18 June 1732, and was won by [[Lycroa]], who defeated [[Emara]] 2–2 ''(4–3 pens)'' in the final at the Fekunza National Stadium in [[Fekunza]] to claim their fourth FLLA World Cup title and equal, at the time, the all-tournament record for most titles held jointly with [[Raledria]]. Twenty-four nations qualified for the final tournament, drawn from the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]], and contested 52 matches across twelve host venues in nine host cities.

The 1732 edition was the first FLLA World Cup held in [[Massir]] and the second contested by twenty-four teams, following the FLLA Council's reintroduction of the 24-team format in 1730 after the [[1728 FLLA World Cup|1728 edition]] in [[Emara]] had reverted on cost grounds to a sixteen-team field. Hosting rights were awarded to [[Dahe]] by the FLLA Council on 18 March 1730 at a meeting in [[Tirna]], the first occasion on which the FLLA Council had selected a host from outside [[Ayuma]], [[Atirha]] or [[New Ayre]]. The format inherited the six-group first round and the supplementary advancement of four third-placed sides from the [[1724 FLLA World Cup|1724 edition]] in [[Areoix Lie]], the inaugural 24-team tournament; the structure would be retained at the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] in [[Verusa]] before being superseded by the 32-team format introduced at the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] in [[Seytinemas]].<ref name="flla-format-1730">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1730/format-resolution|title=FLLA Council resolution 1730/2 on the reintroduction of the 24-team format|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=8 May 1730}}</ref>

The tournament is widely cited in subsequent FLLA literature as the highest-scoring FLLA World Cup of the [[Wikipedia:1730s|1730s]], producing 149 goals across 52 matches at an average of 2.87 per match. The leading goalscoring nation of the tournament was the third-placed side [[Verusa]] with 17 goals across seven matches, ahead of the runners-up [[Emara]] (16 goals) and the [[ATFVL]] qualifier [[Raledria]] (14 goals); the leading individual scorer of the tournament was [[Verusa|Verusan]] forward Wilhelm Brashein with seven personal strikes.

The competition is also remembered for the [[#Final|final]] at the Fekunza National Stadium, in which [[Lycroa]] and [[Emara]] played out a 2–2 draw across normal and extra time before [[Lycroa]] prevailed 4–3 in the resulting penalty shoot-out. The shoot-out was the second in the FLLA World Cup's overall competitive history, following the [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie between [[Emara]] and [[Etretes]] at the [[Qinliya]] Stadium on 5 June, in which [[Emara]] had themselves advanced 7–6 from a thirteen-kick shoot-out after a goalless 120 minutes.<ref name="flla-final-report">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/final-report|title=Match report: 1732 FLLA World Cup final, Lycroa 2–2 (4–3 pens) Emara|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=19 June 1732}}</ref> The hosts [[Dahe]] reached the semi-finals and finished fourth, the landmark performance of the first [[Massir]]-hosted FLLA World Cup and a result that would remain the best by any [[MSFVL]]-affiliated side at an FLLA World Cup until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] in [[Lycroa]].

==Host selection==
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup bids}}

The bid from [[Dahe]] was confirmed as host of the 1732 FLLA World Cup by the [[FLLA]] Council on 18 March 1730 at a meeting held at the FLLA headquarters in [[Tirna]]. The FLLA Council's decision was the first occasion on which an FLLA World Cup had been awarded to a host outside [[Ayuma]], [[Atirha]] or [[New Ayre]] and the first time the [[MSFVL]] confederation had successfully bid for the tournament since its admission to the FLLA in 1685.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1730/host-selection-dahe|title=Dahe confirmed as 1732 FLLA World Cup hosts|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 March 1730}}</ref> Two other associations declared an interest during the bidding window opened in December 1729: [[Sanagara]], the [[MSFVL]]'s strongest international side at the time, and [[Otiiric]], representing the [[MAFVL]] in its first attempt to secure the hosting rights. The [[Sanagara|Sanagaran]] bid was withdrawn on 22 February 1730 after the [[MSFVL]] Executive declined to support two member associations bidding against each other in the same cycle; the [[Otiiric|Otiirican]] bid was rejected by the FLLA Council on cost grounds at the meeting of 18 March 1730.

The [[Dahe|Dahen]] proposal, formally submitted on 4 January 1730 under the umbrella of the [[Dahe|Dahen]] Arraby Federation, was widely understood at the time to have been favoured by the FLLA Council's outgoing president, the [[Praesyu|Praesyuan]] administrator Velan Tomeris, as part of a broader push to extend the competition's geographical reach beyond its three traditional confederations. No formal confederation rotation policy was then in force; under the informal arrangement that had governed the choice of host since the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], the FLLA Council exercised an open discretion subject only to the convention that successive cycles should not be staged on the same continent unless no suitable bid was available from another confederation. The selection of [[Dahe]] returned the tournament to a previously unvisited continent following the [[1728 FLLA World Cup|1728 edition]] in [[Emara]] ([[Ayuma]]) and ahead of the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] in [[Verusa]] ([[Ayuma]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1730/host-selection-procedure|title=FLLA Council procedure for the selection of the 1732 host|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 March 1730}}</ref>

The total infrastructure budget pledged by the [[Dahe|Dahen]] federal government and the participating provincial administrations was {{lahn}}380&nbsp;million, of which {{lahn}}160&nbsp;million was directed towards stadium construction and renovation across the nine host cities, {{lahn}}140&nbsp;million towards transport upgrades (principally the [[Fekunza]]–[[Fekhalai]] coastal railway extension and the new federal highway connecting the [[Qinliya]] and [[Zabantuq]] regions to the capital), and {{lahn}}80&nbsp;million towards operational expenditure including security, broadcasting infrastructure and the volunteer programme.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.darf.dh/1730/budget-statement|title=Federal budget statement of the Dahen Arraby Federation for the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Dahen Arraby Federation|date=4 April 1730}}</ref>

==Format==

The 24 qualified teams were divided into six groups of four for the first round, drawn at the [[#Final draw|final draw]] on 8 December 1731. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing three matches; teams were awarded three points for a win, one for a draw and none for a defeat. The top two teams from each of the six groups advanced directly to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]], joined by the four best third-placed teams ranked across the six groups by total points, then goal difference, then goals scored, then goals scored against, and finally a drawing of lots by the FLLA Organising Committee. The bottom team in each group was eliminated.

In the knockout stage, fixtures were single-elimination ties played over 90 minutes; ties level at the end of normal time were extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]] of two 15-minute halves, with a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] used to decide ties that remained level after extra time. The penalty shoot-out provision had been adopted by the FLLA Council under resolution 1729/7 in advance of the 1732 cycle, replacing the coin-toss provision that had been in force at every FLLA World Cup since the inaugural [[1656 FLLA World Cup|1656 edition]] and that had decided the goalless [[1680 FLLA World Cup|1680 final]] between [[Lycroa]] and [[Eldjo]]. Both semi-final losers contested a [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] on 17 June 1732.<ref name="flla-penalty-resolution">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1729/penalty-resolution|title=FLLA Council resolution 1729/7 introducing the penalty shoot-out|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 November 1729}}</ref>

The 24-team field and six-group format, with four best third-placed teams advancing to a sixteen-team knockout round, were inherited unchanged from the [[1724 FLLA World Cup|1724 edition]] in [[Areoix Lie]], the first FLLA World Cup contested at twenty-four teams; the [[1728 FLLA World Cup|1728 edition]] in [[Emara]] had reverted to the older sixteen-team format on cost grounds before the present 24-team field was reinstated by the FLLA Council in 1730. The 1732 tournament was the second of three FLLA World Cups contested under the 24-team format and the structure would be retained substantially unchanged at the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] in [[Verusa]] before being superseded by the 32-team format introduced at the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] in [[Seytinemas]].<ref name="flla-format-1730" />

==Participating teams==

===Qualification===
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup qualification}}

A total of 24 places at the tournament were allocated across the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]]. Each confederation administered its own qualifying competition, with the format reflecting the size of its membership and its allocation of finals berths. The host association [[Dahe]] qualified as of right under FLLA hosting regulations and did not participate in any [[MSFVL]] qualifying group; no formal host-association exemption from binding qualifying fixtures was yet in force, and the three remaining [[MSFVL]] places at the tournament were therefore competed for by the non-host members of the confederation. The defending champions [[Emara]], winners of the [[1728 FLLA World Cup|1728 edition]] on home soil, qualified through the [[AYFVL]] qualifying competition on merit.

The 1732 qualification programme adopted the berth allocation set by the FLLA Council in 1730: three places to the [[ATFVL]], seven places to the [[AYFVL]], two to the [[NAFVL]], two to the [[MAFVL]], three to the [[QUFVL]], four to the [[MSFVL]] (including the host berth) and three to the [[ACFVL]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1730/berth-allocation-1732|title=Continental berth allocation for the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 October 1730}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/qualification-summary|title=1732 FLLA World Cup qualification: summary by confederation|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=4 May 1732}}</ref> The qualifying tournaments are summarised below; full results are recorded on the individual confederation pages.

==== [[ATFVL]] (Atirha) 3 berths ====
Four first-round groups of five followed by a final octagonal round-robin. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|New Misos}} [[New Misos]]
* {{Flagicon|Raledria}} [[Raledria]]
* {{Flagicon|Genaire}} [[Genaire]]

==== [[AYFVL]] (Ayuma) 7 berths ====
Seven qualifying groups; group winners qualify directly. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|Lycroa}} [[Lycroa]]
* {{Flagicon|Emara}} [[Emara]] ''(defending champions)''
* {{Flagicon|Verusa}} [[Verusa]]
* {{Flagicon|Darewa}} [[Darewa]]
* {{Flagicon|Acrana}} [[Acrana]]
* {{Flagicon|Praesyu}} [[Praesyu]]
* {{Flagicon|Ukhdari}} [[Ukhdari]]

==== [[NAFVL]] (New Ayre) 2 berths ====
A single 23-team double round-robin league. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|United Delet}} [[United Delet]]
* {{Flagicon|Prstreula}} [[Prstreula]]

==== [[MAFVL]] (Mahea) 2 berths ====
Two qualifying groups of twelve teams playing a single round-robin; group winners qualify directly. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|Chaenia}} [[Chaenia]]
* {{Flagicon|Trian}} [[Trian]]

==== [[QUFVL]] (Quia) 3 berths ====
Four first-round groups followed by two qualifying-round-robin groups. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|Finae}} [[Finae]]
* {{Flagicon|Wundry}} [[Wundry]]
* {{Flagicon|Ztesh}} [[Ztesh]]

==== [[MSFVL]] (Massir) 4 berths ====
Four first-round groups followed by two final round-robin groups. The host association [[Dahe]] qualified as of right and also participated in the final round-robin in a non-binding capacity. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|Dahe}} [[Dahe]] ''(host)''
* {{Flagicon|Sanagara}} [[Sanagara]]
* {{Flagicon|Oyreain}} [[Oyreain]]
* {{Flagicon|Etretes}} [[Etretes]]

==== [[ACFVL]] (Acrola) 3 berths ====
Three first-round groups followed by single-leg knockout playoffs. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|Terressin}} [[Terressin]]
* {{Flagicon|Pelines}} [[Pelines]]
* {{Flagicon|Reerica}} [[Reerica]]

===Final draw===
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup seeding}}

The final draw for the first round was held at the [[Fekunza]] Convention Hall on 8 December 1731, six months before the opening match. The 24 qualified teams were divided into four pots of six on the basis of pre-tournament [[FLLA]] rankings, with the host [[Dahe]] and the five highest-ranked sides ([[Raledria]], [[Emara]], [[Lycroa]], [[Verusa]] and [[New Misos]]) placed in the seeded pot. The remaining three pots were arranged on geographical lines so as to maximise the continental diversity of each group; under the procedure adopted by the FLLA Council in October 1731, no group was permitted to contain more than two sides from any one confederation other than the host [[MSFVL]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1731/draw-procedures|title=Procedures for the 1732 FLLA World Cup final draw|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 October 1731}}</ref>

The draw was conducted by FLLA general secretary Vasdari Telmar and presented by [[Dahe|Dahen]] broadcaster Pelai Mwenza, with retired internationals from each of the seven confederations drawing the team names. The ceremony was carried live on Dahen domestic radio and was relayed by 14 broadcasters across more than 40 countries, the broadest relay of any FLLA World Cup draw to that date.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1731/draw-ceremony|title=Official record of the 1732 FLLA World Cup final draw|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 December 1731}}</ref>

===Officials===
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup officials}}

The FLLA Referees Committee appointed 18 refereeing trios, each consisting of one referee and two assistants from the same national association, and three support pairs drawn from a combined pool of 12 nations. The selections were announced between October 1731 and February 1732, following an assessment programme at senior friendlies organised across the nine host cities. The 18 selected referees were drawn from 13 nations and represented all seven [[FLLA]] confederations, although no [[MSFVL]] referee was eligible to take charge of any match involving a [[MSFVL]] side under the host-association exclusion rules then in force.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/officials-announced|title=Match officials confirmed for the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 February 1732}}</ref>

The opening match was refereed by Dietmar Karlavi of [[Estijan]] ([[AYFVL]] support pair), appointed to the fixture in his fourth tournament as an international referee. The final was officiated by Henrik Olstrad of [[Eldjo]] ([[AYFVL]]), the first [[Eldjo|Eldjoan]] referee to take charge of an FLLA World Cup final since [[1668 FLLA World Cup|1668]]. The two semi-finals were taken by Tomáš Novák of [[Otiiric]] ([[MAFVL]]) for the first semi-final at the [[Qinliya]] Stadium and Diego Hernández of [[Astye]] ([[NAFVL]] support pair) for the second semi-final at the [[Zabantuq]] Stadium.

==Squads==
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup squads}}

Each participating squad consisted of 22 players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers, under the squad allocation adopted by the FLLA Council in 1730 and retained at every subsequent FLLA World Cup. Each participating national association was required to confirm its final 22-player squad with the FLLA no later than seven days before the opening match; late replacements were permitted in the event of serious injury at any time up to 24 hours before a team's first fixture. A total of 528 players were registered for the tournament, of whom 48 were goalkeepers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.darf.dh/1732/squad-rules|title=Squad regulations for the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Dahen Arraby Federation|date=12 May 1732}}</ref>

The oldest player at the tournament was [[Emara|Emaran]] central defender Korv Maladin, who was 36 years and 142 days old at the start of the competition; the youngest was the [[Wundry|Wundric]] forward Sanjar Halaki at 19 years and 84 days. The mean age of registered players across the tournament was 26.8 years.

The [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] central midfielder Cario Velarzo, then 21 years old, was making his first appearance at an FLLA World Cup and would go on to set the all-tournament record for repeat appearances by a single player at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]], representing his country also at the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736]] and [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 editions]] before lifting the trophy as captain of the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] champions of 1744. The [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] captain at the 1732 tournament was central defender Olari Verzini, then 31 years old and at his second FLLA World Cup, who would retire from international football following the conclusion of the tournament. The hosts [[Dahe]] were captained by central midfielder Linwei Pung, then 29 years old, and were managed by Bavalu Khan, in his first tournament as the Dahen head coach.

==Venues==
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup venues}}

Twelve stadiums in nine host cities were used in the final tournament, all located in [[Dahe]]. Four of the twelve venues had been built specifically for the tournament or substantially redeveloped during the bidding period; the remaining eight were existing top-flight venues that received targeted upgrades to seating and broadcasting facilities under FLLA Council resolution 1730/6. The twelve-venue programme was the largest single-host stadium plan in the competition's history at the time, exceeded only by the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 twelve-venue programme]] in [[Verusa]] four years later and by the larger plans introduced under the 32-team format from the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] onwards.

The opening match was held at the Fekunza National Stadium in [[Fekunza]], the largest and most prestigious stadium in the host country, which also staged one quarter-final on 10 June and the final on 18 June. The two semi-finals were divided between the [[Qinliya]] Stadium and the [[Zabantuq]] Stadium. The third-place playoff was held at the [[Tsinjara]] Stadium.

===Venue profiles===

The '''Fekunza National Stadium''', in [[Fekunza]], was the largest venue at the tournament and the principal final venue. The stadium, designed by the architectural studio Wuyani Limited and inaugurated by the head of state of [[Dahe]] on 12 February 1732, was constructed on the southern bank of the [[Fekunza]] coastal estuary and replaced the older Fekunza City Ground (closed 1729) as the regular home venue of the [[Dahe]] national side.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.darf.dh/venues/fekunza-national|title=Fekunza National Stadium: history, design and inauguration|publisher=Dahen Arraby Federation|date=12 February 1732}}</ref> The 75,000-seat ground hosted the [[#Final|final]], one of the four [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-finals]] on 10 June, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie (between the hosts [[Dahe]] and [[Terressin]]), and three first-round fixtures including the opening match between [[Dahe]] and [[Praesyu]] on 22 May.

The '''Fekhalai Sports Park''' in [[Fekhalai]], the country's largest city, was the second-largest venue at the tournament with a redeveloped capacity of 65,000 and the principal eastern venue. The ground, originally opened in 1714 and extensively redeveloped between 1730 and 1732, hosted one [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] on 11 June, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, and three first-round fixtures. The '''[[Qinliya]] Stadium''' in [[Qinliya]], a 50,000-seat venue opened in 1720 as the home of the local domestic-league club Qinliya United, hosted the first of the two [[#Semi-finals|semi-finals]] between [[Lycroa]] and [[Dahe]] on 14 June, the [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie between [[Emara]] and [[Etretes]] (the first penalty shoot-out in the FLLA World Cup's competitive history), and three first-round fixtures.

The '''[[Zabantuq]] Stadium''' in [[Zabantuq]], a 48,000-seat venue opened in February 1732 specifically for the tournament, hosted the second [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]] between [[Emara]] and [[Verusa]] on 14 June, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, and three first-round fixtures. The '''[[Tsinjara]] Stadium''' in [[Tsinjara]], a 42,000-seat venue completed in November 1731 in commemoration of the centenary of the federal reorganisation of the [[Tsinjara]] province, hosted the [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] between [[Dahe]] and [[Verusa]] on 17 June, one [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] on 11 June, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, and three first-round fixtures.

The '''[[Mouyein]] Stadium''' in [[Mouyein]], a 40,000-seat ground purpose-built for the tournament and inaugurated on 4 March 1732, staged one [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]], one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie and three first-round fixtures. The remaining six venues, the Fekunza Civic Ground, the Fekunza North Park, the Fekhalai Eastern Stadium, the Yandala Stadium, the Khuazhin Stadium and the Tayoluni Stadium, between them staged two further [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] ties and nineteen first-round fixtures.

===Team base camps===

Each of the 24 participating squads selected a base camp from a shortlist of 28 candidate sites circulated by the Dahen Arraby Federation in October 1731. Most teams opted for camps in or around the larger host cities, with five squads basing themselves within a one-hour radius of [[Fekunza]] and four near [[Fekhalai]]. The remaining fifteen were divided between the smaller host cities and the inland highland corridor between [[Mouyein]] and [[Yandala]], which became known during the tournament as the "Wuyani belt" after the architectural studio that had overseen the regional camp-conversion programme.

==Opening ceremony==

The opening ceremony of the 1732 FLLA World Cup was held at the Fekunza National Stadium on 22 May 1732, sixty minutes before the kick-off of the opening match between the hosts [[Dahe]] and [[Praesyu]]. Directed by [[Dahe|Dahen]] stage producer Kweli Mwenza and choreographed by Lena Lufuliya, the ceremony lasted 30 minutes and featured 680 dancers, 160 musicians and a massed entrance representing each of the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]]. The performance opened with a sequence drawing on the migration routes of the [[Dahe|Dahen]] coastal peoples across the [[Massir|Massiran]] interior, before transitioning to a portrayal of the seven confederations arrayed as a single concentric ring around the centre circle in a deliberate echo of the opening sequence of the [[1724 FLLA World Cup|1724 edition]] in [[Areoix Lie]]. The [[Dahe|Dahen]] vocalist Mbali Tayoluni, joined by the Fekunza Choral Society, performed the tournament's official theme song "Zolisha Lwandle" ("Across the Inland Sea") as the closing item of the ceremony.

Attending dignitaries included the head of state of [[Dahe]], the President of the FLLA Council, the heads of state of [[Sanagara]] and [[Vesozata]], and 38 ambassadors and senior diplomatic representatives. The ceremony was broadcast live on radio by 14 partner broadcasters across 28 countries; a transcontinental relay arranged in coordination with the broadcasting consortium that had carried the [[1728 FLLA World Cup|1728 final]] enabled the opening ceremony to be heard in real time across most of [[Atirha]], [[Ayuma]] and the eastern half of [[Massir]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dnb.dh/1732/opening-ceremony|title=Opening ceremony of the 1732 FLLA World Cup: production notes and broadcast record|publisher=Dahen National Broadcaster|date=22 May 1732}}</ref>

==First round==

The 24 qualified teams were drawn into six groups of four. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing three matches; the top two finishers in each group advanced directly to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]], joined by the four best of the six third-placed sides ranked across the groups. Group rankings were settled first on points (three for a win, one for a draw), then on goal difference and goals scored.

The first round was a notably open and high-scoring phase of the competition, producing 108 goals across 36 matches at an average of exactly 3.00 per match. The hosts [[Dahe]] topped a tightly contested Group B in which all four sides finished within a point of each other, advancing on goal difference and head-to-head record above [[Oyreain]] (also four points) and [[Praesyu]] (four points, advancing as a third-placed team). [[Verusa]] took the only perfect first-round record of the round with three wins from three in Group F, while [[Lycroa]] in Group A and [[Emara]] in Group D advanced as group winners with seven points apiece. The single highest-scoring fixture of the round was the 6–6 draw between [[Raledria]] and [[Etretes]] at the Mouyein Stadium on 26 May, the highest-scoring single-match draw in the competition's history at the time and one of three group-stage fixtures in which both sides scored four or more goals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/group-stage-summary|title=1732 FLLA World Cup first round: results summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=3 June 1732}}</ref>

All times listed are Standard Dahen Time ([[wikipedia:UTC|UTC]]+3).

===Ranking of third-placed teams===

The four best of the six third-placed sides were ranked across all groups by points, goal difference and goals scored, and joined the twelve group winners and runners-up in the round of sixteen. The four sides advancing were [[Etretes]] (Group C), [[Genaire]] (Group A), [[Praesyu]] (Group B) and [[Terressin]] (Group E); the remaining two third-placed sides, [[New Misos]] (Group D) and [[Acrana]] (Group F), were eliminated.

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the sixteen teams that advanced from the first round. Matches still level after 90 minutes were extended by a 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; if scores remained tied after extra time, the tie was decided by [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] under the provision adopted by the FLLA Council in 1729.<ref name="flla-penalty-resolution" /> One of the eight round-of-sixteen ties required a penalty shoot-out, one of the four quarter-finals required additional time, the first semi-final required a penalty shoot-out, the third-place playoff required additional time, and the [[#Final|final]] itself was decided on penalties after a 2–2 draw across normal and extra time. The cumulative goal total of 41 across the sixteen knockout matches at 2.56 per match contrasted markedly with the open scoring of the first round and reflected the more cautious tactical orientation of the leading sides as they entered the knockout phase.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/knockout-summary|title=1732 FLLA World Cup knockout stage: results summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=19 June 1732}}</ref>

===Round of 16===

The six group winners and six group runners-up were joined by the four highest-ranked third-placed sides at the round of 16. The fixture pairings were settled in advance under the published bracket structure approved by the FLLA Organising Committee in November 1731. One of the eight round-of-sixteen ties was decided by a penalty shoot-out, the first such resolution in the FLLA World Cup's competitive history; six further ties were settled by a margin of one or two goals. The highest-scoring fixture of the round was [[Raledria]] 4–3 [[Sanagara]] at the Fekhalai Sports Park, in which the [[Raledria|Raledrian]] forward Aurelian Sundas, who four years later would lead the leading-scorer table at the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]], scored two of his side's goals.

===Quarter-finals===

The four quarter-finals produced three results decided inside 90 minutes and one in extra time. [[Lycroa]] beat [[Raledria]] 1–0 at the Fekunza National Stadium in a tight contest settled in the 71st minute by a long-range strike from [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] forward Halvor Marzeti, his fourth goal of the tournament. The hosts [[Dahe]] beat [[Ukhdari]] 3–2 at the [[Tsinjara]] Stadium in the only home win for an [[MSFVL]] side at a non-MSFVL knockout fixture of the tournament, captain Linwei Pung's 89th-minute winner sealing a [[Dahe|Dahen]] place in the semi-finals. [[Emara]] beat [[Genaire]] 4–0 at the Fekhalai Sports Park, the most one-sided quarter-final in the FLLA World Cup since the [[1720 FLLA World Cup|1720 edition]], with [[Emara|Emaran]] forward Tomaz Renari scoring two of his side's goals. [[Verusa]] beat [[Finae]] 4–3 at the [[Mouyein]] Stadium after a 3–3 draw at the end of normal time and a single decisive goal in the 108th minute from forward Wilhelm Brashein, his fifth goal of the tournament.

===Semi-finals===

The first semi-final at the [[Qinliya]] Stadium produced the second penalty shoot-out of the tournament: the hosts [[Dahe]] and [[Lycroa]] played out a 0–0 draw across normal time and extra time, [[Dahe]] surviving for long periods on the defensive against a [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] side that took 17 shots to [[Dahe]]'s seven across the 120 minutes. The tie was decided by a penalty shoot-out, in which [[Lycroa]] prevailed 5–2 after [[Dahe|Dahen]] captain Linwei Pung, forward Bharikai Zhao and central midfielder Khalozi all missed their kicks for the hosts while every [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] kick was converted. The win gave [[Lycroa]] their first FLLA World Cup final appearance since the [[1720 FLLA World Cup|1720 edition]] in [[Etirha]], at which the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] side had lost the final 4–0 to [[Praesyu]]. The [[Dahe|Dahen]] elimination at the semi-final stage equalled the best result by any first-time host of an FLLA World Cup and would remain the high-water mark of an [[MSFVL]] performance at an FLLA World Cup until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] in [[Lycroa]].

The second semi-final at the [[Zabantuq]] Stadium was a fluctuating attacking contest in which [[Emara]] beat [[Verusa]] 3–2 across 90 minutes, the most goals scored in a knockout fixture of the tournament after the round-of-sixteen rounds. [[Emara]] led at half-time through goals from Vidoma Calreth (12th minute) and Tomaz Renari (38th minute) but were pulled back to 2–2 by 67 minutes through a Wilhelm Brashein double; an 82nd-minute strike from [[Emara|Emaran]] central midfielder Estori Lavanti, deflected past [[Verusa|Verusan]] goalkeeper Reinmar Brashen at the near post, settled the result. The win gave [[Emara]] their first FLLA World Cup final appearance since the [[1716 FLLA World Cup|1716 edition]] in [[Easuhura]], at which the [[Emara|Emaran]] side had been defeated 2–1 by [[Raledria]].

===Third place playoff===

The third-place playoff was contested between the two losing semi-finalists at the [[Tsinjara]] Stadium on 17 June. [[Verusa]] beat the hosts [[Dahe]] 1–0 after extra time, the only goal of the match scored in the 102nd minute by [[Verusa|Verusan]] forward Wilhelm Brashein from a low cross by left-back Werner Mokshlein. The result was Brashein's seventh and final goal of the tournament, settling his position as the leading individual scorer of the competition, and gave [[Verusa]] their third top-three FLLA World Cup finish in four editions following the [[1720 FLLA World Cup|1720]] (third-place) and [[1724 FLLA World Cup|1724]] (champions) tournaments. [[Dahe]]'s fourth-place finish remained the high-water mark of an [[MSFVL]] performance at an FLLA World Cup until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] in [[Lycroa]].

===Final===
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup final}}

The final was contested between [[Lycroa]] and [[Emara]] on 18 June 1732 at the Fekunza National Stadium in [[Fekunza]] in front of an attendance of 74,800, the highest single-match attendance at any FLLA World Cup match to that date. The final was the first FLLA World Cup final to be contested between the two highest-scoring sides of the qualifying phase since the [[1672 FLLA World Cup|1672 edition]] in [[Emara]] and the first to feature two [[AYFVL]] sides since the [[1720 FLLA World Cup|1720 edition]] in [[Etirha]]. [[Lycroa]] entered the match having scored eleven goals across their six previous fixtures and conceded seven; [[Emara]] had reached the final having scored fourteen goals across the same number of matches, against a defensive record of just three goals conceded.

[[Lycroa]] took an early lead through forward Halvor Marzeti in the 14th minute, the forward picking up a low cross from captain Olari Verzini at the near post and finishing under [[Emara|Emaran]] goalkeeper Ortes Mavari for his fifth goal of the tournament. [[Emara]] equalised in the 36th minute through a header from forward Tomaz Renari from a corner taken by central midfielder Estori Lavanti, his sixth goal of the tournament. [[Emara]] took the lead in the 67th minute through a low strike from captain Vidoma Calreth, but [[Lycroa]] levelled in the 84th minute through a powerful header by central midfielder Renar Reltari from a corner taken by left-back Mateo Solar.<ref name="flla-final-report" /> The match remained 2–2 through the two halves of extra time, with both sides defending in increasingly compact shapes and producing only a single shot on target between them across the 30-minute additional period.

The tie was decided by a penalty shoot-out, the second in the FLLA World Cup's overall competitive history following the [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen tie]] between the same [[Emara]] side and [[Etretes]] at the [[Qinliya]] Stadium on 5 June. [[Lycroa]] won the shoot-out 4–3 after [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] forward Halvor Marzeti scored the first kick and [[Emara|Emaran]] forward Tomaz Renari opened with a goal in reply; both sides converted their second and third kicks before [[Emara|Emaran]] central defender Korv Maladin saw his fourth kick saved low to the left by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] goalkeeper Renar Carestano, the only save of the shoot-out. [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] central midfielder Cario Velarzo, who had been substituted on in the 78th minute of normal time, converted [[Lycroa]]'s fourth and decisive kick to seal the result. The win gave [[Lycroa]] their fourth FLLA World Cup title, equalling at the time the all-tournament record held jointly with [[Raledria]] and confirming the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] domestic generation of the late 1720s as the most successful in the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] Arraby Federation's history to that date.<ref name="flla-final-report" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lnb.ly/sport/1732/final|title=Lycroa win fourth world title in Fekunza shoot-out|publisher=Lycroan National Broadcaster|date=18 June 1732}}</ref>

==Statistics==

===Goalscoring===

[[Verusa]] finished as the tournament's leading goalscoring nation with 17 goals across seven matches, ahead of the runners-up [[Emara]] (16 in seven) and the [[ATFVL]] qualifier [[Raledria]] (14 in five). The overall goal-per-match average of 3.90 across 52 matches was, at the time, the highest at any FLLA World Cup since the [[1708 FLLA World Cup|1708 edition]] in [[United Delet]] and the only edition between the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]] and the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] to exceed an average of 3.5 goals per match. The figure was later cited in the FLLA Secretariat's [[#Aftermath|1737 review]] (drafted in response to the lower-scoring [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] in [[Verusa]]) as evidence of the heights of attacking football that the 24-team format could produce when no defensive consensus had yet formed among the leading sides.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/goalscoring-summary|title=1732 FLLA World Cup goalscoring summary by nation|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 June 1732}}</ref>

===Top individual scorers===

The tournament produced no formal individual goalscorer's award. The competition's modern top-scorer prize, the [[FLLA Marskval]], was not adopted in its current form until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]]; at the 1732 tournament the FLLA's Goalscoring Secretariat published a leading-scorer table at the conclusion of the competition without a formal trophy or presentation. The 1732 leading individual scorer was [[Verusa|Verusan]] forward Wilhelm Brashein with seven personal strikes, ahead of [[Emara|Emaran]] forward Tomaz Renari and [[Finae|Finaean]] forward Daron Veshani with six goals each.

===Discipline===

The FLLA Disciplinary Committee issued a total of 156 yellow cards and 11 red cards across the 52 matches of the tournament, an average of 3.00 yellows and 0.21 reds per match. The most-cautioned team was [[Raledria]], with 14 yellow cards and 2 reds across their five matches; [[Reerica]] received the fewest among the participating teams, with two yellows and no reds across their three first-round matches. Three players received red cards in the knockout stage: [[Ukhdari|Ukhdari]] central defender Vornsai in the 83rd minute of the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] against the hosts [[Dahe]] at the [[Tsinjara]] Stadium for a second bookable offence, [[Genaire|Genairean]] central midfielder Carreta in the 78th minute of the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] against [[Emara]] for serious foul play, and [[Verusa|Verusan]] left-back Werner Mokshlein in the 119th minute of the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] against [[Finae]] for violent conduct (Mokshlein was suspended for the [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]] against [[Emara]] as a result).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/discipline/1732-summary|title=FLLA Disciplinary Committee report on the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=10 August 1732}}</ref>

==Awards==

The 1732 FLLA World Cup did not formally award any of the individual prizes that are now associated with the modern competition. The current top-scorer award (the [[FLLA Marskval]]) and best-goalkeeper award (the [[FLLA Bastion]]) were both adopted in their present form only at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]]; the Best Young Player Award was introduced at the [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752 edition]]; and the FLLA Fair Play Trophy was introduced at the [[1756 FLLA World Cup|1756 edition]]. The FLLA's Goalscoring Secretariat published an unofficial leading-scorer table at the conclusion of the 1732 tournament, and a small panel of seven sports journalists drawn from each of the seven confederations published an unofficial best-player citation, but neither was accompanied by a formal trophy or a presentation at the closing ceremony.

The unofficial best-player citation, published on 25 June 1732 by a panel led by the [[Praesyu|Praesyuan]] sports journalist Mares Antellor, was awarded to [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] forward Halvor Marzeti, who scored five goals across the tournament including the opening goal of the [[#Final|final]] and converted the first [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] kick of the final shoot-out. The unofficial leading-scorer citation, published the same day by the FLLA Goalscoring Secretariat, was awarded to [[Verusa|Verusan]] forward Wilhelm Brashein with seven personal strikes. Both citations were retrospectively recognised by the FLLA in 1745 as the predecessors of the modern [[FLLA Vairan Ball]] and [[FLLA Marskval]] awards but neither holder is listed among the formal winners of either prize.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1745/awards-historical-recognition|title=Historical recognition of pre-1744 best-player and leading-scorer citations|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 February 1745}}</ref>

==Preparations and costs==

The total budget allocated to the 1732 FLLA World Cup by the Dahen Arraby Federation and the federal government of [[Dahe]] was {{lahn}}380&nbsp;million. Of this, {{lahn}}160&nbsp;million was directed towards stadium construction and renovation across the twelve venues, {{lahn}}140&nbsp;million towards transport upgrades (principally the [[Fekunza]]–[[Fekhalai]] coastal railway extension and the new federal highway connecting the [[Qinliya]] and [[Zabantuq]] regions to the capital), and {{lahn}}80&nbsp;million towards operational expenditure including security, broadcasting infrastructure and the volunteer programme. Per-venue capital costs averaged {{lahn}}13.3&nbsp;million across the twelve stadiums, the lowest figure recorded at any FLLA World Cup since the [[1716 FLLA World Cup|1716 edition]] in [[Easuhura]].

Four of the twelve venues, the Fekunza National Stadium, the [[Zabantuq]] Stadium, the [[Tsinjara]] Stadium and the [[Mouyein]] Stadium, were newly built for the tournament; the remaining eight were existing top-flight venues that received targeted upgrades to seating and broadcasting facilities. The newest, the Fekunza National Stadium, was inaugurated on 12 February 1732, just over three months before the opening match; cost escalation during the final stages of construction added {{lahn}}18&nbsp;million to the projected budget for the venue, absorbed in full by the federal government under a guarantee provision agreed with the Dahen Arraby Federation at the bid stage.

The combined security operation involved 9,000 police and federal personnel deployed across the nine host cities. No serious incidents were reported during the competition. A dedicated public-transport extension programme, providing free local-network travel to ticket holders for the day of each match, was introduced for the duration of the tournament and was retained by the [[Fekunza]] municipal authority as a permanent matchday provision following the closing ceremony.

Total tournament revenue, audited by the FLLA in August 1732, was {{lahn}}620&nbsp;million, against costs of {{lahn}}380&nbsp;million, yielding a net surplus of {{lahn}}240&nbsp;million. The FLLA's standard 15&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent host-association allocation returned {{lahn}}93&nbsp;million to the Dahen Arraby Federation, which was retained in full by the federation under the single-host allocation formula then in force.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/audit/1732-final-accounts|title=Audited final accounts of the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 August 1732}}</ref>

==Marketing==
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup marketing}}

The marketing programme for the 1732 FLLA World Cup was overseen by the Dahen Arraby Federation in partnership with the FLLA's commercial division, with creative direction by the [[Fekunza]]-based studio Wuyani Limited. The programme included the official emblem, mascot, match ball and theme song (see [[#Symbols|Symbols]] below), a domestic travelling-trophy tour that visited 12 cities across [[Dahe]] in the year preceding the tournament, and a tiered sponsorship structure of three worldwide partners, five host-nation partners and three regional supporters. Total sponsorship revenue across all three tiers was {{lahn}}170&nbsp;million, then the highest gross sponsorship figure recorded by any FLLA World Cup.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/commercial/1732-sponsorship|title=1732 FLLA World Cup commercial and sponsorship summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=10 September 1732}}</ref>

==Symbols==
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup symbols}}

===Emblem===

The official emblem of the tournament, designed by the [[Fekunza]]-based studio Wuyani Limited, was unveiled on 14 May 1731 in a public ceremony at the Dahen National Auditorium in [[Fekunza]]. The design depicts a stylised silhouette of the [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]] rising from a representation of the southern [[Massir|Massiran]] coastline, framed by a triple-helix device drawn from the heraldry of the [[Dahe|Dahen]] coastal provinces and intended to symbolise the host nation's reception of the global tournament. The emblem received the FLLA Council's formal endorsement in September 1731 after a three-week consultation period with the seven confederations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1731/emblem-endorsement|title=FLLA Council endorses official emblem of the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 September 1731}}</ref>

===Mascot===

The official mascot of the 1732 FLLA World Cup, named '''Zoluni''', is an anthropomorphic Dahen waterbuck ([[wikipedia:Waterbuck|Kobus ellipsiprymnus]]) dressed in the blue-and-yellow panel jersey representing the national colours of [[Dahe]]. The mascot was selected by a domestic public vote organised by the Dahen Arraby Federation in the summer of 1731, with three candidate designs presented to voters across the host nation and in print; Zoluni prevailed over a stylised river crocodile ("Hambazo") and an anthropomorphic Dahen lion ("Tholan") with 47&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent of the 1.2 million votes cast.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.darf.dh/1731/mascot-vote|title=Zoluni named official mascot of 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Dahen Arraby Federation|date=14 August 1731}}</ref>

===Match ball===

The official match ball, manufactured by the [[Fekhalai]]-based sports-equipment maker Xiyanja Athletics, was branded the '''Lwandle''' (literally "ocean", a reference to the [[Massir|Massiran]] coastline along which the principal host city sat). The Lwandle featured a 32-panel hand-stitched construction in a blue-and-yellow livery and was the first FLLA World Cup match ball to use the 32-panel hand-stitched construction that would become the standard from the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] onwards. A distinct silver-coloured version of the ball, the Lwandle Silver, was used in the [[#Final|final]], the [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] and the two [[#Semi-finals|semi-finals]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.xiyanja.dh/products/lwandle-1732|title=Lwandle and Lwandle Silver: official match balls of the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Xiyanja Athletics|date=14 February 1732}}</ref>

===Trophy===

The 1732 FLLA World Cup was contested under the one-trophy [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]] arrangement that had been in continuous operation since the inaugural [[1656 FLLA World Cup|1656 edition]] and that would remain in force for one further edition, the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 tournament]] in [[Verusa]], before being replaced by the present two-trophy system at the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]]. The Ayuma Cup, a 24-centimetre gilded silver sculpture depicting a stylised laurelled figure holding a single sphere aloft, was presented to the winners of each completed edition as a permanent transfer, with the holding nation retaining the cup until the conclusion of the next tournament. [[Lycroa]] received the Ayuma Cup at the closing ceremony of the [[#Final|final]] on 18 June 1732 from the FLLA Council president and retained the trophy until the spring of 1736, when it was returned to the FLLA Secretariat ahead of the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] in [[Verusa]] for presentation to its eventual winners.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/ayuma-cup|title=The Ayuma Cup: history and current display|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=4 January 1740}}</ref>

[[Lycroa]]'s receipt of the Ayuma Cup at the 1732 tournament was the fourth occasion on which the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] federation had lifted the trophy following the [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660]], [[1668 FLLA World Cup|1668]] and [[1680 FLLA World Cup|1680 editions]], and equalled at the time the all-tournament record for receipt of the cup then held jointly by [[Raledria]] (1700, 1712, 1716). The shared record was later broken by [[Lycroa]] alone at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] in [[Lycroa]] itself, when the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] champions lifted the new rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]] for the first time alongside the bespoke permanent trophy of that edition, the [[FLLA World Cup#Permanent trophies|Caltarra]].

===Theme song===

The official theme song of the tournament, "Zolisha Lwandle" ("Across the Inland Sea"), was composed by [[Dahe|Dahen]] composer Tholiwe Zolaman with lyrics jointly written by Zolaman and the vocalist Mbali Tayoluni, who also performed the track. The studio recording was released on 4 April 1732 and topped the [[Dahe|Dahen]] domestic charts across the months of May and June 1732; it was the first sports-themed track to lead the [[Dahe|Dahen]] charts in the recording era and was retained in heavy rotation across [[Dahe|Dahen]] domestic radio for much of the year following the tournament.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.darf.dh/charts/1732-june|title=Dahen domestic chart summary, June 1732|publisher=Dahen Recording Industry Association|date=4 July 1732}}</ref>

==Media==
{{Main|1732 FLLA World Cup broadcasting rights}}

The 1732 FLLA World Cup was broadcast in 42 countries by 14 official radio partners. Domestic broadcasting rights in [[Dahe]] were held by the Dahen National Broadcaster (DNB), which produced the host radio feed and broadcast all 52 matches across its terrestrial radio network. The international rights for the [[AYFVL]] region were held by the [[Emara|Emaran]] public-service broadcaster ENB; the [[ATFVL]] rights by the Raledrian National Broadcaster (RNB); and the [[MSFVL]] rights by a four-broadcaster consortium led by the Sanagaran National Network (SNN).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/broadcasting-rights|title=1732 FLLA World Cup: international broadcasting partners|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 April 1732}}</ref>

The 1732 edition was the first FLLA World Cup at which the live radio commentary for every fixture of the tournament was carried by a single transcontinental relay; the relay arrangement, extending the partial arrangement first used at the [[1728 FLLA World Cup|1728 edition]], enabled audiences across all seven confederations to listen to every match as it was played. The FLLA reported a cumulative live broadcast audience for the tournament of 180 million individual listeners across all matches, with 85 million individuals tuning in to at least part of the [[#Final|final]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/audience-summary|title=1732 FLLA World Cup viewership summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 August 1732}}</ref>

===Attendance===

Cumulative attendance across the 52 matches of the tournament was 1,948,000 spectators, an average of 37,462 per match. The highest single-match attendance was the 74,800 recorded at the [[#Final|final]] between [[Lycroa]] and [[Emara]] at the Fekunza National Stadium in [[Fekunza]], just below the venue's listed all-seater capacity of 75,000; the lowest was the 28,400 attending the Group D fixture between [[New Misos]] and [[Reerica]] at the [[Khuazhin]] Stadium on 28 May.

Across the tournament, attendance averaged 46,800 in the knockout stage and 33,400 in the first round. The three highest single-match attendances of the tournament were all recorded at the Fekunza National Stadium, with the final, the QF1 between [[Lycroa]] and [[Raledria]] and the round-of-16 fixture between [[Lycroa]] and [[Praesyu]] all drawing crowds in excess of 72,000.

==Controversies==

The most prominent dispute of the tournament arose from the [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie between [[Emara]] and [[Etretes]] at the [[Qinliya]] Stadium on 6 June, in which [[Emara]] advanced 7–6 on penalties after a goalless 120 minutes in the FLLA World Cup's first-ever penalty shoot-out. The [[Etretes|Etretes]] Arraby Federation lodged a written protest with the FLLA Refereeing Committee on 8 June, contending that the [[Eldjo]] referee Henrik Olstrad had failed to apply the laws of the game then in force when permitting the [[Emara|Emaran]] forward Mavari to retake his fifth kick after an alleged step-back violation by [[Etretes|Etretes]] goalkeeper Brakan; the FLLA Refereeing Committee dismissed the protest on 12 June and issued a published clarification of the relevant provision of the laws on 22 June 1732, a clarification that was reissued in materially identical terms at the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] following a similar dispute in the round of sixteen between [[Ealdorii]] and [[Quidic]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/referees/1732/etretes-decision|title=FLLA Refereeing Committee decision on Etretes protest of 8 June 1732|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 June 1732}}</ref>

A second dispute, of a sporting character, arose from the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] between [[Verusa]] and [[Finae]] at the [[Mouyein]] Stadium on 11 June, in which [[Verusa|Verusan]] left-back Werner Mokshlein was sent off in the 119th minute of extra time for violent conduct after an altercation with [[Finae|Finaean]] forward Daron Veshani. The [[Verusa|Verusan]] Arraby Federation lodged a written submission with the FLLA Disciplinary Committee on 12 June, contending that the dismissal had been the product of an inadvertent reaction by Mokshlein to repeated provocation by Veshani; the [[Verusa|Verusan]] submission was dismissed on 13 June and Mokshlein's suspension for the [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]] against [[Emara]] was upheld. The [[Verusa|Verusan]] side, depleted by Mokshlein's absence at the [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]], were eliminated 3–2 by [[Emara]] at the [[Zabantuq]] Stadium two days later.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/discipline/1732/mokshlein-suspension|title=FLLA Disciplinary Committee decision on the Mokshlein dismissal|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=13 June 1732}}</ref>

A third dispute, of an administrative rather than sporting character, arose from the host-association exclusion rules then in force in respect of the [[Dahe|Dahen]] support pair refereeing trio, which had been forced to withdraw from a number of MSFVL-side matches that the Refereeing Committee had originally proposed. The Dahen Arraby Federation contended in correspondence with the FLLA Secretariat on 2 July 1732 that the exclusion rules, as drafted, had imposed a disproportionate burden on the host association without any obvious sporting benefit; the FLLA Council took notice of the correspondence at its meeting of 14 October 1732 but declined to revise the exclusion rules ahead of the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1732/host-exclusion-correspondence|title=Dahen Arraby Federation correspondence on host-association referee exclusion|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 October 1732}}</ref>

==Aftermath==

[[Lycroa]]'s victory was their fourth FLLA World Cup title, equalling at the time the all-tournament record then held jointly with [[Raledria]] and confirming the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] domestic generation of the late 1720s as the most successful in the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] Arraby Federation's history to that date. The result was widely celebrated across [[Lycroa]], where the team's homecoming reception at the [[Jungui]] central square on 21 June 1732 drew an estimated crowd of 920,000 along a three-kilometre route from the [[Jungui]] railway station to the federal palace.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lnb.ly/news/1732/homecoming-reception|title=Lycroan homecoming reception draws 920,000 to Jungui|publisher=Lycroan National Broadcaster|date=21 June 1732}}</ref> As reigning champions, [[Lycroa]] qualified for the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|subsequent 1736 edition]] through the [[AYFVL]] qualifying competition on merit, no formal defending-champion exemption then being in force; [[Lycroa]] would be eliminated in the round of sixteen at the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 tournament]] by [[Easuhura]] after their famous 3–2 group-stage defeat at the hands of the [[QUFVL]] qualifier [[Wundry]].

Across the host nation, the tournament was judged a substantial organisational success, the first FLLA World Cup ever held in [[Massir]] having delivered both a record-equalling fourth title for [[Lycroa]] and a landmark semi-final run for the inaugural [[MSFVL]] host. An independent post-event report commissioned by the Dahen federal government and published in October 1732 estimated the net economic contribution to the host economy at {{lahn}}890&nbsp;million, against gross public expenditure of {{lahn}}380&nbsp;million across infrastructure and operations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.dh/1732/wc-economic-impact|title=Independent post-event economic impact report on the 1732 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Federal Government of Dahe|date=22 October 1732}}</ref> International visitor arrivals across [[Dahe]] over the tournament period totalled 280,000, the highest cumulative tournament-period visitor figure recorded in [[Massir]] up to that date. The matchday public-transport provision introduced for the tournament was retained on a permanent basis after the closing ceremony by the municipal authorities of [[Fekunza]] and [[Fekhalai]].

The tournament's open and high-scoring character, with a goal-per-match average of 3.90 across 52 matches, contrasted markedly with the lower-scoring [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] in [[Verusa]] (2.69 goals per match) and was later cited in the FLLA Secretariat's 1737 review as evidence of the range of tactical orientations that the 24-team format could produce. The 1737 review's recommendation that the field be expanded to 32 teams, adopted by the FLLA Council under resolution 1737/3 in April 1737, drew on the contrast between the 1732 and [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 editions]] as one of several arguments in favour of broadening the technical diversity of the participating field. The penalty shoot-out provision introduced for the 1732 edition under FLLA Council resolution 1729/7 was retained at every subsequent FLLA World Cup and remains the standard tie-breaking procedure in the modern competition.<ref name="flla-penalty-resolution" />

The next edition of the FLLA World Cup, the [[1736 FLLA World Cup]], was awarded to a single-nation bid from [[Verusa]] at the FLLA Council meeting of 4 March 1734, returning the tournament to [[Ayuma]] under the informal alternation that governed host selection at the time. [[Raledria]] would win the 1736 tournament under the same 24-team format, defeating the hosts [[Verusa]] 3–1 in a final at the Estadio Vulime in [[Huifarn]] remembered for an unusual 36-minute floodlight stoppage in the 53rd minute.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1734/1736-host-confirmation|title=Verusa confirmed as 1736 FLLA World Cup hosts|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=4 March 1734}}</ref>
